messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meera is a 23-year-old UX designer, married and living in a quiet suburb with her husband. Eight months ago, while driving home from a late shift, she struck a pedestrian who stepped suddenly into the crosswalk. The man—middle-aged, with a dark beard and a worn leather jacket—survived but suffered severe leg fractures and a traumatic brain injury. Meera remembers the thud, the way his body folded over her hood, the paramedics’ voices. She has not driven since.

At work, Meera is surrounded by triggers. Her open-plan office is filled with people who move unpredictably, and every time a colleague walks past her desk, her stomach tightens. She finds herself scanning the room for anyone who looks like the man she hit—a similar build, a similar jacket—and when she spots someone, her heart races and she feels dizzy. To cope, she has developed a set of strategies that she relies on daily. She tries hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the memory down when it surfaces, but this suppression only makes the thoughts return more insistently, like a spring she cannot keep compressed. She also dwells on how the event could have been prevented, replaying the moment over and over: *If I had left five minutes later. If I had checked the crosswalk again.* This rumination, she believes, might help her avoid ever making the same mistake, but it keeps the scene vivid and the guilt fresh.

Her avoidance of driving has reshaped her life. She takes the train to work, a commute that doubles her travel time, and she has stopped visiting her parents, who live an hour away, because the thought of being a passenger on the highway makes her feel like she might vomit. Her husband has become her chauffeur for errands, and he has begun to express frustration that she cannot “just get over it.” Meera has come to believe that she is fundamentally irresponsible—that the accident proves she is careless and dangerous, a person who should not be trusted behind a wheel. This appraisal fuels her hypervigilance at work, where she monitors every movement around her, certain that if she is not constantly on guard, she will cause another catastrophe.

The cycle tightens. The more she suppresses and ruminates, the more sensitive she becomes to triggers. A man with a dark beard walking past her desk sends her into a spiral of self-blame, and she retreats to the bathroom to breathe through her hands. She has started to avoid certain floors of the office building, taking the stairs instead of the elevator, because a colleague on the third floor has the same jacket as the victim. Her productivity has slipped, and her manager has noticed. Meera is terrified that she will be fired, and she is equally terrified that if she stops monitoring herself, she will hurt someone again.

She finally sought help after a panic attack in the break room last week. A coworker found her shaking and called her husband, who took her home. Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Meera is most afraid of one thing: that she will never feel safe in her own skin again. She hopes, quietly, that someone can teach her how to stop the replaying—to let the memory be just a memory, not a sentence she serves every day.
